title: Chloroplast ionome characterization provides new avenues to shape organellar iron homeostasis
content: While only needed in small quantities, mineral nutrients and trace elements are essential for plants to perform normal physiological functions. The entire set of these inorganic elements, known as the ionome, was characterized in Arabidopsis thaliana more than 20 years ago and since then has shaped our understanding of plant nutrition (Lahner et al. 2003). Tissues, cell types and even intracellular compartments display remarkably distinct mineral levels (Giehl et al. 2023). For instance, chloroplasts have a relatively high demand for manganese (Mn), copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn), and are the main sink for iron (Fe) in leaf cells (Terry and Low 1982). Almost all plant nutrient deficiencies disrupt chloroplast ion homeostasis, impairing photosynthesis, growth and yield (Kunz et al. 2024). Thus, an in-depth understanding of their ionome composition and homeostasis is crucial to develop biotechnological strategies that protect plants under nutrient stress and enhance essential mineral nutrients in crops (biofortification). However, quantitative data on chloroplast elemental composition remains selective and limited, especially from model plants.
